The village of Santiago Zamora near Antigua is associated with Kaqchikel Maya culture. Visitors learn about traditional handicraft techniques and meet people who continue to practice them. Textiles and crafts as part of everyday community life are the main focus of a visit.

The village is home to a group of women artisans called "Ixoqi' Aj Q'ijema." Meeting them offers an opportunity to see how their products are made and how patterns and craftsmanship relate to the region's culture. A visit to Santiago Zamora complements time spent in Antigua and San Antonio Aguas Calientes, revealing the traditions of communities beyond the colonial city.

In Santo Antônio, visitors discover everyday life in an Amazonian community. A visit to the village is combined with a walk through the equatorial forest and a boat ride.

This stop forms part of a route through the communities of Santo Antônio and Tiririca. The program shows how daily life is connected to the river and the surrounding forest.

In Mexico City's Plaza de Santo Domingo, the facade's red stone is set against pale carved details. The church recalls a large Dominican monastery, of which only part of the buildings have survived.

Inside, the altars and side chapels attract attention. Our Lady of the Rosary and Our Lady of Covadonga are venerated here; prayer and an appreciation of religious art become part of the same visit. The church is easy to include in a walk through the historic center alongside the Zócalo and Metropolitan Cathedral. This is the church in the capital: the church of the same name with its Chapel of the Rosary in Puebla is in another city.
